title.rendered: PIND, ColdHubs unveil solar cold hub to preserve farm produce

content.rendered:
The Foundation for Partnership Initiatives in the Niger Delta and ColdHubs Limited have inaugurated a solar-powered cold storage and ice-making facility at Swali Market in Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, to reduce post-harvest losses and improve incomes for farmers, fisherfolk and traders.

Developed by ColdHubs Limited with support from PIND’s Coastal Communities Off-Grid Energy Challenge Fund, the facility runs on a 44kWp solar photovoltaic system with 240kWh battery storage.

The project includes a walk-in cold room and a solar-powered ice-making unit capable of producing up to one tonne of ice daily for fisherfolk, food traders, smallholder farmers and other businesses operating within Swali Market and neighbouring communities.

The organisations said the intervention will reduce food losses, improve product quality, raise incomes, cut reliance on diesel-powered refrigeration and expand access to clean energy.

Speaking during the inauguration, the Executive Director of PIND, Sam Daibo, said the project demonstrated the role of renewable energy in driving economic growth and strengthening livelihoods.

He said, “This facility demonstrates that renewable energy is more than a source of electricity, it is a catalyst for livelihoods, enterprise growth, and economic resilience. By supporting innovative businesses like ColdHubs, PIND is helping to build stronger market systems that reduce losses, increase incomes, and improve food security across the Niger Delta.”

The Founder and Chief Executive Officer of ColdHubs Limited, Nnaemeka Ikegwuonu, said the partnership will expand access to reliable cold-chain infrastructure for underserved communities.

“For many small-scale producers, the lack of reliable cold storage translates directly into lost income. This partnership with PIND enables us to bring sustainable, solar-powered cold chain solutions closer to the people who need them most, helping preserve food quality, reduce waste, and improve livelihoods,” Ikegwuonu said.

A fish trader at Swali Market, Charity Ochiezi, said the facility will improve business operations by reducing spoilage: “Before now, we lost a large portion of our fish because we had no affordable way to preserve them. This facility will help us keep our products fresh for longer, reduce spoilage, and increase our earnings.”

PIND said the Swali Market project forms part of its Access to Energy and Market Systems Development programmes aimed at improving agricultural and fisheries value chains, boosting productivity and expanding economic opportunities across the Niger Delta.

The foundation added that the project provides a scalable model for reducing post-harvest losses, improving food security and creating sustainable livelihoods in rural and coastal communities by combining renewable energy with market-driven innovation.
